usage: polite; opens your view to anyone
반말; to a friend or younger person
제 생각에는 좀 다른 것 같아요
I think it's a bit different
examples: 제 생각에는 괜찮아요.
In my opinion, it's fine.
the bare opener leading into a short view
제 생각에는 지금 가는 게 좋을 것 같아요.
I think it'd be better to go now.
everyday use; pairs with -는 게 좋을 것 같다 to stay soft
제 생각에는 이 방법도 좋지만, 시간이 좀 더 필요할 것 같아요.
In my opinion this method is good too, but I think we'd need a bit more time.
fuller view in a discussion; hedges before raising a concern
nuance: 제 생각에는 is the standard polite way to flag 'this is just my view' before you state an opinion, used learner-to-anyone in conversation, meetings, or class. 제 is the humble 'my' (저+의), and the particle 에는 frames it as 'as for in my thinking'. To go casual with a friend, swap to 내 생각에는; for a more weighed, formal feel use 제 생각으로는. The nearest alternative is 제가 보기에는 ('the way I see it'), but 제 생각에는 is about your reasoning/opinion while 제가 보기에는 leans on what you observe — name that line: thinking vs seeing. The classic English-speaker mistake is calquing 'in my opinion' as 제 의견에는, which sounds stiff and is rarely said; spoken Korean overwhelmingly uses 제 생각에는. Another is dropping the particle and saying 제 생각 괜찮아요, which is ungrammatical — keep 에는.

Omitting the particle (제 생각 좋아요) — you need 제 생각에는 / 제 생각엔; the bare noun can't open the clause this way.

english: The way I see it / From what I can tell...
usage: polite; offering a judgment from observation
제가 보기에는 별문제 없을 것 같아요
I don't think it'll be a problem
examples: 제가 보기에는 괜찮은데요.
From what I can see, it looks fine.
the bare judgment, softened by -는데요
제가 보기에는 이게 더 나아 보여요.
The way I see it, this one looks better.
everyday comparison; ties to 보다 'to look'
제가 보기에는 가격은 비슷한데 디자인이 더 마음에 들어요.
The way I see it, the price is similar but I like the design more.
fuller real opinion weighing two options
nuance: 제가 보기에는 means 'judging from what I see/observe', used when you give an assessment based on appearances or your read of a situation — learner to anyone, polite. It's built on 보다 'to see' + 기 (nominalizer) + 에는, literally 'as for in my seeing'. Casual form is 내가 보기에는; the contracted 제가 보기엔 is very common in speech. The nearest neighbor is 제 생각에는 — the dividing line is evidence vs opinion: 제가 보기에는 implies 'from observable signs', while 제 생각에는 is your inner reasoning. English speakers often force 제 의견으로는 or translate 'I see' too literally; also they may say 제가 봤을 때 (past, 'when I looked') when they mean the general present judgment 제가 보기에는. Keep it present and nominalized.

examples: 네, 맞아요.
Yes, that's right.
confirming a fact someone stated
맞아요, 저도 어제 그 뉴스 봤어요.
Right, I saw that news yesterday too.
agreeing and adding your own experience
아, 맞아요! 그 카페 주말엔 문을 일찍 닫더라고요.
Oh, that's right! That cafe closes early on weekends.
remembering/confirming with -더라고요 reporting what you noticed
nuance: 맞아요 (from 맞다 'to be correct/to fit') confirms that what the other person said is true, used learner-to-anyone in polite speech; it's the everyday 'right / exactly'. Casual is 맞아 and formal is 맞습니다 (service staff, presentations). The nearest alternative is 그래요 / 그렇죠 — the line is: 맞아요 judges a statement as factually correct, while 그래요/그렇죠 expresses general agreement or 'yeah, that's how it is'. The biggest English-speaker trap is treating 맞아요 like 'okay/sure' for requests — for 'okay, I'll do it' you need 알겠어요 / 좋아요, not 맞아요. Another pitfall: answering a negative question. To Korean '안 더워요?' ('Isn't it hot?'), 맞아요 is confusing; Koreans answer the literal proposition, so be careful. Note 맞다 is intransitive here, so never say 맞아요 하다 — 맞아요 stands alone.

usage: polite; seeking or giving shared agreement
rising tone to invite the listener to agree
examples: 그렇죠.
Exactly.
agreeing with what was just said
요즘 진짜 덥죠? — 그렇죠, 너무 더워요.
It's really hot lately, right? — Right, it's so hot.
agreeing with a -죠 question and amplifying
그렇죠, 사실 저도 처음엔 좀 망설였는데 하길 잘했어요.
Right, honestly I hesitated at first too, but I'm glad I did it.
agreeing then sharing a fuller personal take
nuance: 그렇죠 (from 그렇다 'to be so' + the 죠 ending) expresses warm, shared agreement — 'right, that's how it is' — used learner-to-anyone in polite conversation. The 죠 (contraction of 지요) seeks mutual confirmation, so 그렇죠 often feels like nodding along with someone. Casual is 그렇지; formal is 그렇습니다. The nearest alternative is 맞아요 — the dividing line: 맞아요 confirms a statement is factually correct, while 그렇죠 signals empathetic 'yeah, exactly' and is great for small talk and building rapport. With a rising tone 그렇죠? invites the other person to agree with YOU. English speakers often overuse 맞아요 where 그렇죠 sounds warmer, and they sometimes write 그렇죠 as two thoughts; also beware spelling — it's 그렇죠, not 그러죠 (the ㅎ stays).

usage: I agree with that opinion too
extension naming what you agree with
examples: 네, 동의해요.
Yes, I agree.
agreeing with a proposal or opinion
그 점에는 저도 동의해요.
I agree with you on that point.
agreeing with one specific point; note 점에는
전반적으로는 동의하는데, 일정만 조금 조정하면 좋겠어요.
I agree overall, but I'd just like to tweak the schedule a bit.
agreeing in principle while raising one reservation
nuance: 동의해요 (동의[同意] 'agreement' + 해요) is a slightly formal 'I agree', used learner-to-anyone but most at home in discussions, meetings, or when reacting to an opinion or proposal. Casual is 동의해; formal is 동의합니다. The nearest everyday alternative is 저도 그렇게 생각해요 ('I think so too') or 맞아요 — the dividing line: 동의해요 sounds like agreeing with a position/argument (a bit bookish), while 저도 그렇게 생각해요 is warmer and more conversational, and 맞아요 just confirms correctness. The particle matters: you agree WITH something using 에, so 그 의견에 동의해요, not 그 의견을 동의해요 — this 을/를 error is the single most common English-speaker mistake (English says 'agree something/agree with'). For casual chat among friends, 동의해요 can feel stiff; 맞아, 내 말이 sound more natural.

examples: 저도 그렇게 생각해요.
I think so too.
agreeing after someone shares a view
맞아요, 저도 그렇게 생각해요. 가격이 좀 비싼 것 같아요.
Right, I think so too. The price seems a bit high.
agreeing and adding a reason
사실 저도 그렇게 생각했어요. 근데 막상 써 보니까 생각보다 괜찮더라고요.
Honestly I thought so too. But once I actually used it, it was better than expected.
agreeing about a past view, then nuancing
nuance: 저도 그렇게 생각해요 ('I too think like that') is the warm, conversational way to agree with someone's opinion, used learner-to-anyone in polite speech. 저도 = 'me too', 그렇게 = 'like that/so', 생각해요 = 'think'. Casual is 나도 그렇게 생각해; formal 저도 그렇게 생각합니다. The nearest alternatives are 동의해요 and 저도 같은 생각이에요 — the dividing line: 저도 그렇게 생각해요 is the everyday spoken default (friendly, opinion-based), 동의해요 is more formal/argument-based, and 저도 같은 생각이에요 is a touch more polished. The key English-speaker mistake is saying 저도 생각해요 (dropping 그렇게), which just means 'I think too' and is incomplete — you need 그렇게 to mean 'think SO'. Also note 저도 already carries 'too', so don't add another 'also'.

Adding a redundant 또 ('also') — 저도 already means 'me too'; 저도 또 그렇게 생각해요 is doubled.

usage: trailing off to signal doubt or polite refusal
examples: 글쎄요.
Hmm, I'm not sure.
non-committal reply to a question
주말에 시간 돼요? — 글쎄요, 한번 봐야 할 것 같아요.
Are you free this weekend? — Hmm, I'll have to see.
polite hedging on a request
글쎄요, 그건 좀 더 생각해 봐야 할 것 같아요.
Well, I think I need to think about that a bit more.
buying time before committing to an opinion
nuance: 글쎄요 is the go-to hedge for 'hmm, I'm not sure / let me think', used learner-to-anyone in polite speech when you don't want to commit, don't know, or are gently declining. Casual is 글쎄. Crucially it's not just 'I don't know' — it signals hesitation or reservation, so Koreans use it to soften a 'no' or to avoid a direct answer without seeming rude. The nearest alternative is 잘 모르겠어요 — the dividing line: 잘 모르겠어요 literally means 'I don't know well (a fact)', while 글쎄요 is attitudinal hedging ('I'm noncommittal / I have doubts'). English speakers wrongly treat 글쎄요 as a casual 'whatever' or use it where a clear answer is expected (a boss asking a direct work question), which can read as evasive. It is polite but vague — use it when vagueness is acceptable.

Spelling it 글세요 — it's 글쎄요 with double ㅆ.

english: I'm not sure / I don't really know.
usage: extension when you also lack the answer
examples: 잘 모르겠어요.
I'm not really sure.
honest reply to a question you can't answer
이거 어떻게 하는 거예요? — 어, 저도 잘 모르겠어요.
How do you do this? — Oh, I'm not sure either.
admitting you don't know, sharing the uncertainty
솔직히 아직 잘 모르겠어요. 좀 더 알아보고 말씀드릴게요.
Honestly I'm not sure yet. Let me look into it and get back to you.
polite 'I don't know yet' plus a follow-up promise
nuance: 잘 모르겠어요 is the natural, polite 'I'm not sure / I don't really know', used learner-to-anyone. Note two things English speakers miss: first, Koreans say 잘 ('well') + 모르겠어요, so it's literally 'I don't know well' — adding 잘 makes it softer and more natural than a bare 몰라요, which can sound blunt or even cold. The nearest alternative is 글쎄요 — the line: 잘 모르겠어요 honestly reports lack of knowledge, while 글쎄요 is noncommittal hedging. The big mistake is using bare 몰라요 in answer to someone (especially a request), which sounds curt; soften to 잘 모르겠어요. Also don't translate 'I don't know him' with 모르겠어요 — for not knowing a person use 몰라요 (잘 몰라요).

english: That doesn't seem right / I don't think that's okay.
usage: that's not really okay, I think
that's not really okay, is it?
extension inviting agreement on the objection
examples: 음, 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요.
Hmm, I don't think that's okay.
softly rejecting an idea
그렇게 말하는 건 좀 아닌 것 같아요.
I don't think it's right to say it like that.
gently objecting to someone's behavior
취지는 이해하는데, 그렇게까지 하는 건 좀 아닌 것 같아요.
I get the intention, but I don't think going that far is right.
acknowledging then disagreeing about going too far
nuance: 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 ('that seems a bit not-right') is how Koreans disagree or disapprove POLITELY without a blunt 'no', used learner-to-anyone. The machinery is key: 아니다 'to not be (so)' + -ㄴ 것 같다 'seems' softens it to opinion, and 좀 ('a bit') cushions the blow — together they let you object while saving face. Casual is 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아; formal 그건 좀 아닌 것 같습니다. The nearest alternative is 저는 반대예요 ('I'm against it') — the dividing line: 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 is gentle, indirect, situational disapproval, while 저는 반대예요 is a clear, on-the-record objection (meetings, votes). The classic English-speaker mistake is bald directness — saying 그건 틀렸어요 ('that's wrong') or 안 돼요 to disagree, which feels harsh and confrontational in Korean. Keep 좀 and 것 같아요 to stay polite. Also note it's 아닌 (from 아니다), not 안 인.

mistakes: Disagreeing with 그건 틀렸어요 ('that's wrong') — too blunt/confrontational; soften to 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요.
Dropping 좀 and 것 같아요 (그건 아니에요) — that's much harsher; the hedges are what make it polite.
Writing 안인 것 같아요 — the correct form from 아니다 is 아닌 것 같아요.

english: That's true, but... / That may be so, however...
usage: 반말; same form works with a friend
examples: 그렇긴 한데...
That's true, but...
conceding a point before objecting
그렇긴 한데, 가격이 좀 부담돼요.
That's true, but the price is a bit much for me.
agreeing in part, then raising a concern
네, 그렇긴 한데, 그래도 한 번 더 확인해 보는 게 좋지 않을까요?
Yes, that's true, but still, wouldn't it be better to double-check?
conceding, then politely pushing your view
nuance: 그렇긴 한데 is the 'yes, but...' move — you concede the other person has a point, then pivot to your reservation, used learner-to-anyone. The grammar: 그렇다 + -긴 하다 (the -기는 하다 'it IS so, granted' concession pattern) + -ㄴ데 ('but/and'). So it literally grants 'it is indeed so, but'. This same form is used in 반말 and 존댓말 (the politeness lives in what follows); the formal version is 그렇긴 합니다만. The nearest alternative is 그럴 수도 있죠 ('that could be so') — the line: 그렇긴 한데 actively concedes then disagrees, while 그럴 수도 있죠 merely allows the possibility without committing. English speakers often jump straight to 하지만/그러나 ('but/however') with no concession, which sounds abrupt and argumentative; 그렇긴 한데 cushions disagreement by agreeing first. Mistake to avoid: writing 그렇긴 한대 (wrong ending) instead of 한데.

english: It's not great / I don't really like it.
usage: I don't think it's that great
examples: 음... 별로예요.
Hmm... it's not that great.
giving a mildly negative verdict
그 영화 어땠어요? — 솔직히 좀 별로였어요.
How was that movie? — Honestly, it wasn't that great.
everyday opinion in past tense 별로였어요
맛은 괜찮은데 서비스는 좀 별로였어요.
The food was okay, but the service was kind of disappointing.
splitting a verdict: one part fine, one part 별로
nuance: 별로예요 is the everyday way to say something is 'not that great / meh', a softly negative opinion used learner-to-anyone. 별로 originally means 'particularly' and pairs with negatives, but in speech 별로예요 stands alone as 'it's nothing special'. Casual is 별로야; the hedged 별로인 것 같아요 is gentler; past is 별로였어요 (after you've tried it). The nearest alternative is 그저 그래요 ('so-so') — the line: 별로예요 leans clearly negative ('I don't like it'), while 그저 그래요 is neutral 'meh, average'. The top English-speaker mistakes: (1) spelling — it's 별로예요, never 별로에요 (after a noun-like 별로 the copula is 예요); (2) overusing 별로 as a strong 'bad' — it's mild, so for genuinely bad use 안 좋아요/별로 안 좋아요; (3) saying 별로 좋아요 — 별로 must go with a negative, so it's 별로 안 좋아요 or just 별로예요.

english: I think so / It seems that way.
examples: 네, 그런 것 같아요.
Yes, I think so.
softly confirming without full certainty
오늘 비 올까요? — 그런 것 같아요. 하늘이 어둡네요.
Will it rain today? — Seems like it. The sky is dark.
inferring from evidence
다들 그 의견에 찬성하는 것 같아요. 분위기를 보니 그런 것 같아요.
Everyone seems to be for that idea. From the mood, it seems so.
reading a situation and hedging the conclusion
nuance: 그런 것 같아요 ('it seems to be so') is the soft, hedged 'I think so', used learner-to-anyone constantly — Koreans love -ㄴ/는 것 같다 because it states opinions tentatively and politely instead of asserting flatly. Casual is 그런 것 같아; formal 그런 것 같습니다. The nearest alternatives are the confident 맞아요/그렇죠 — the dividing line: 그런 것 같아요 hedges ('seems so, I'm not 100% sure'), while 맞아요/그렇죠 confirm with confidence. This hedging is a politeness device: even when fairly sure, Koreans soften with 것 같아요 to avoid sounding pushy. The English-speaker mistake is over-asserting — saying 그래요 or 맞아요 where 그런 것 같아요 would sound more modest and natural — or, conversely, misusing 것 같다 about their OWN clear feelings (saying 좋은 것 같아요 'it seems good' when you simply like it; that's actually common and fine, but for strong personal certainty 좋아요 is more direct). Also: it's 그런 것, two words, not 그런것.

Confusing 그런 것 같다 (seems so) with 그렇다 (is so) — the 것 같다 version is tentative on purpose.

usage: extension showing you just realized/accept it
examples: 그럴 수도 있죠.
That could be.
allowing a possibility you hadn't considered
사람마다 다르니까 그럴 수도 있죠.
People are different, so that's possible.
conceding because of individual variation
그럴 수도 있죠. 근데 저라면 좀 다르게 했을 것 같아요.
That's possible. But if it were me, I think I'd have done it differently.
acknowledging, then offering your own take
nuance: 그럴 수도 있죠 ('that could be so, right') concedes that something is possible without fully committing to it, used learner-to-anyone in polite speech. The build: 그렇다 → 그럴 (prospective) + 수도 있다 ('it's possible, even') + 죠 (seeking shared acknowledgment). It's a diplomatic, open-minded reaction — 'fair enough, that's possible'. Casual is 그럴 수도 있지; formal 그럴 수도 있습니다. The nearest alternative is 그렇긴 한데 — the dividing line: 그럴 수도 있죠 grants a possibility neutrally (no pushback implied), while 그렇긴 한데 concedes specifically in order to then disagree. English speakers tend to translate 'maybe' as 아마 and miss this concession nuance, or overuse 가능해요 ('it's possible/feasible'), which is more about feasibility than 'I'll grant you that'. Keep the 수도 있다 frame; spacing is 그럴 수도 있죠 (수 is spaced).

mistakes: Saying 가능해요 to mean 'that could be (in conversation)' — 가능하다 is about feasibility; for granting a point use 그럴 수도 있죠.
Writing 그럴수도 있죠 — 수 is a bound noun and is spaced: 그럴 수도 있죠.
Forcing 아마 ('maybe/probably') in its place — 아마 estimates likelihood; 그럴 수도 있죠 concedes a possibility someone raised.

examples: 저는 반대예요.
I'm against it.
stating clear opposition to a proposal
미안하지만 저는 반대예요. 위험할 것 같아서요.
Sorry, but I'm against it. I think it could be risky.
polite opposition with a reason
다들 찬성하시는 것 같은데, 저는 솔직히 반대예요.
Everyone seems to be in favor, but honestly I'm against it.
voicing a minority objection in a group
nuance: 저는 반대예요 ('I'm against it') is the clear, on-the-record way to disagree with a proposal or position, used learner-to-anyone but typical in meetings, planning, or votes. 반대[反對] = 'opposition'; 찬성[贊成] = 'approval/being for' is its antonym. Casual is 나는 반대야; formal 저는 반대합니다. The nearest alternative is 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 — the dividing line: 저는 반대예요 is explicit, committed opposition (you're stating a stance), while 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 is gentle, indirect disapproval that avoids a hard 'no'. Because direct opposition can feel strong in Korean, soften with 미안하지만 ('sorry, but') or add a reason (-아서/어서). The particle is 에: you oppose something with 그 의견에 반대예요, not 그 의견을 반대예요. English speakers calque 'I disagree' as 저는 동의 안 해요 (understandable but flatter) or use the wrong particle 을/를 — keep 에.

mistakes: Saying 그 의견을 반대예요 — 반대(하다) takes 에: 그 의견에 반대예요.
Opposing bluntly with no cushion — add 미안하지만 or a reason (-아서요) so it doesn't sound combative.
Confusing 반대 with 반대로 — 반대로 means 'on the contrary/in reverse'; for 'I'm against it' it's 저는 반대예요.

examples: 좋은 생각이에요!
That's a good idea!
endorsing a suggestion enthusiastically
같이 점심 먹을까요? — 좋은 생각이에요.
Shall we have lunch together? — Good idea.
accepting a suggestion warmly
회의를 오전으로 옮기자고요? 좋은 생각이에요. 그게 더 효율적일 것 같아요.
Move the meeting to the morning? Good idea. I think that'd be more efficient.
endorsing and backing it with a reason
nuance: 좋은 생각이에요 ('that's a good thought') endorses someone's suggestion or idea, used learner-to-anyone in polite speech — a friendly, positive reaction. 좋은 (from 좋다 'good') + 생각 'thought/idea' + 이에요. Casual is 좋은 생각이야; with -네요 (좋은 생각이네요) it adds a touch of fresh realization. The nearest alternative is 좋아요 ('sounds good / okay') — the dividing line: 좋은 생각이에요 specifically praises the IDEA as clever/sensible, while 좋아요 just signals general assent ('sure, fine'). For accepting a plan, both work, but 좋은 생각이에요 is warmer about the suggestion itself. English speakers sometimes say 좋은 아이디어예요 (using the loanword 아이디어), which is fine and common, but 좋은 생각이에요 is the more native default. Watch the copula spelling: after the consonant-ending 생각, it's 생각이에요, not 생각에요.

Saying 좋는 생각 — 좋다 is an adjective, so the modifier is 좋은, not 좋는.
Reducing it to bare 좋아요 when you mean to praise the idea — 좋아요 is general assent; 좋은 생각이에요 compliments the idea itself.

english: What I mean is... / My point is...
usage: polite; clarifying or restating your point
격식; raising your humility a notch
what I mean is, it's not that
examples: 아니, 제 말은...
No, what I mean is...
restarting to clarify after being misread
제 말은, 지금 당장 하자는 게 아니에요.
What I mean is, I'm not saying we should do it right now.
clarifying to prevent a misunderstanding
제 말은 그게 아니라, 순서를 좀 바꾸면 어떨까 하는 거예요.
My point isn't that — it's that maybe we could change the order a bit.
correcting and then restating the real suggestion
nuance: 제 말은 ('as for my words/what I'm saying') is how you clarify, restate, or rescue your point when you've been misunderstood, used learner-to-anyone in polite speech. 제 = humble 'my', 말 = 'words/speech', 은 = topic particle. Casual is 내 말은; the humble-formal 제 말씀은 raises deference. It very often precedes 그게 아니라 ('it's not that') to correct a misreading: 제 말은 그게 아니라.... The nearest alternative is 그러니까 ('so / what I'm saying is') — the dividing line: 그러니까 reframes/continues your reasoning, while 제 말은 explicitly re-centers on YOUR intended meaning, usually after a misunderstanding. English speakers calque 'I mean' as 제가 의미하는 건, which is unnatural; spoken Korean uses 제 말은. Also, don't confuse 말 with 말씀 in the wrong direction: 말씀 is humble/honorific and 제 말씀은 elevates your own speech politely toward a senior.
